t.2.34.1: But having heard Rāma's words and having seen him wearing the garb of an ascetic, the king, together with his wives, lost consciousness.
t.2.34.2: Consumed by grief, he did not look at Rāghava; and, sick at heart, he did not look upon him and speak to him in reply.
t.2.34.3: For a moment the mighty-armed lord of the earth lay as if senseless, and, stricken with grief, he lamented, thinking only of Rāma.
t.2.34.4: Surely, I think, in some former time I deprived many of their young, or else did harm to living creatures; that is why this has come upon me.
t.2.34.5: But life does not depart from the body before its appointed time has come; though I am tormented by Kaikeyī, death does not come to me.
t.2.34.7: Indeed, it is on account of Kaikeyī alone that these people are made to suffer, she who, resorting to this deceit, strives for her own advantage.
t.2.34.6: I am the one who sees standing before me my own son, radiant as fire, who has cast off his two fine garments and is clad in the covering of an ascetic.
t.2.34.8: Having spoken these words, his senses clouded by tears, he uttered "Rāma!" just once and could say nothing more.
t.2.34.9: Having regained consciousness after a moment, that lord of the earth, with eyes filled with tears, spoke these words to Sumantra.
t.2.34.10: Yoke the royal carriage with the finest horses and come here; then convey this greatly fortunate one beyond the borders of this realm.
t.2.34.11: This, I think, is what is called the fruit of the virtues of the virtuous: that a good and heroic man is banished to the forest by his father and mother.
t.2.34.12: Understanding the king's command, Sumantra, swift in his stride, yoked the adorned chariot with horses and came there.
t.2.34.13: The charioteer, joining his palms in reverence, announced to the king's son that the chariot, adorned with gold and yoked with the finest horses, was ready.
t.2.34.14: The king, who knew the right place and time, quickly summoned the man in charge of amassing wealth and spoke to him decisively, with words pure in every respect.
t.2.34.16: Thus addressed by the lord of men, he went then to the treasury, gathered all of it, and quickly gave it to Sītā.
t.2.34.15: Costly garments and excellent ornaments, enough for these years by your reckoning, bring quickly for Vaidehī.
t.2.34.17: That well-born Vaidehī, setting out for the forest, adorned her well-formed limbs with those many-hued ornaments.
t.2.34.18: Richly adorned, Vaidehī made that dwelling shine, just as the radiance of Vivasvant, the rayed one, lights up the sky at the time of his rising.
t.2.34.19: Embracing her with both arms and kissing on the head Maithilī, who was not acting in a pitiable or unworthy way, her mother-in-law spoke these words.
t.2.34.20: Throughout this whole world, unfaithful women, though constantly honored with kindnesses, do not stand by a husband who has fallen into misfortune.
t.2.34.21: My son, though he has been sent into exile, must not be slighted by you; let him be your god, whether he is without wealth or possessed of wealth.
t.2.34.22: Having understood her words, which were in accord with dharma and with what is beneficial, Sītā, standing before her mother-in-law with hands joined in reverence, spoke these words to her.
t.2.34.23: I shall do everything that the noble lady instructs me. I know how one ought to conduct oneself toward a husband, and I have heard it taught as well.
t.2.34.24: The noble lady should not count me among the wicked; I can no more stray from dharma than radiance can depart from the moon.
t.2.34.25: A vīṇā without strings cannot be played, a chariot without wheels does not move; so too a woman without a husband does not prosper in happiness, even though she may have a hundred sons.
t.2.34.26: A father gives in measure, a mother gives in measure, a son gives in measure; what woman would not honor her husband, the giver of what is beyond measure?
t.2.34.28: Hearing Sītā's heart-touching words, Kausalyā, pure of spirit, suddenly shed tears born of both sorrow and joy.
t.2.34.27: Being such as I am, of noble standing, and having learned dharma in all its higher and lower aspects, how could I disregard him, noble lady? For to women the husband is a deity.
t.2.34.29: Approaching with joined palms his mother, who was highly honoured in the midst of the mothers, Rāma, supreme knower of dharma, spoke these words to her.
t.2.34.30: Mother, do not grieve; look after my father. For the end of my dwelling in the forest will come very soon.
t.2.34.31: Even as you sleep, nine years and five will pass, and then you will see me arrived here safe and whole, surrounded by my friends.
t.2.34.32: Having spoken to his mother these words so full of fitting sense, he looked about and saw his mothers, three hundred and fifty in number.
t.2.34.33: And to those mothers, who were likewise stricken with grief, the son of Daśaratha, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words in keeping with dharma.
t.2.34.34: Whatever harsh thing I may have done through our living together, or even out of ignorance, pardon me for it; and I take leave of you all.
t.2.34.35: Then, as Rāghava spoke thus, there arose from the wives of the lord of men a loud clamour, like the cry of female krauñca birds.
t.2.34.36: The palace of Daśaratha, which once resounded like thunderclouds with the sound of murajas and paṇavas, now became filled with weeping and lamentation, overtaken by calamity and plunged into deep sorrow.
